reason: The sources provide 18 verified claims with multiple eyewitness and administrative accounts detailing the mud-soaked tragedy, English longbow tactics, and casualties.
story: On October 25, 1415, a starving, disease-ridden English army under King Henry V faced annihilation in northern France. Outnumbered and trapped, the English withdrew to a narrow field of recently ploughed land hemmed in by dense forests. Heavy rain had turned the soil into a swamp of thick, knee-deep mud. The French launched a massive cavalry and armored infantry charge, but it was a disaster. Under a terrifying hail of longbow arrows, the heavily armored French knights sank into the muck. The crush of their own advancing ranks pushed them together so tightly they could not even swing their swords. Many suffocated under the weight of their own falling comrades or drowned inside their helmets. Sensing a desperate opportunity, lightly equipped English archers dropped their bows and slaughtered the trapped knights with hammers and axes. In the tragic chaos, Henry ordered the execution of thousands of prisoners before claiming a miraculous, legendary victory.
angle: The heavily armored French knights were packed so tightly in the knee-deep mud that they could not swing their weapons, causing many to suffocate under their own falling comrades or drown inside their helmets.

claims.claim: The Battle of Agincourt took place on October 25, 1415, near Azincourt in northern France.

evidence.quote: It took place on 25 October 1415 (Saint Crispin's Day) near Azincourt, in northern France.
At Agincourt, a clearing in the woods of Tramecourt near the village of Azincourt (the exact location is unknown).

claims.claim: King Henry V's army initially landed in northern France with approximately 12,000 men.

evidence.quote: The army of about 12,000 men and up to 20,000 horses besieged the port of Harfleur.
Henry and his army of 12,000 men sailed to Northern France and landed on August 13th.

claims.claim: The English army's numbers were severely depleted by disease during the campaign.

evidence.quote: many soldiers died from disease, and the English numbers dwindled during the Siege of Harfleur;
the siege took far too long and resulted in many diseases spreading throughout the British camp.

claims.claim: The English army marched 260 miles (420 km) to find a crossing over the Somme River.

evidence.quote: had marched 260 miles (420 km) in two and a half weeks,
Henry marched his exhausted men 420 km (260 miles) south over the next two weeks, desperate to find a crossing;

claims.claim: The French army was commanded by Constable Charles d'Albret.

evidence.quote: The French were commanded by Constable Charles I d'Albret
faced 25,000 French men under Constable Charles d’Albret.

claims.claim: The battlefield was extremely muddy due to recent heavy rain on recently ploughed land.

evidence.quote: Recent heavy rain had made the battlefield very muddy,
the recently-plowed ground – churned up by the recent rain – was thick with mud.

claims.claim: English archers drove pointed wooden stakes into the ground to protect themselves from cavalry.

evidence.quote: The English and Welsh archers on the flanks drove pointed wooden stakes, or palings, into the ground at an angle to force cavalry to veer off.
When in position, they drove sharpened stakes into the ground to protect themselves from the French horsemen.

claims.claim: King Henry V fought directly to protect his wounded brother, the Duke of Gloucester.

evidence.quote: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester had been wounded in the groin, Henry took his household guard and stood over his brother, in the front rank of the fighting, until Humphrey could be dragged to safety.
slashed his way towards the Duke of Gloucester and saved him from a group of French knights.

claims.claim: King Henry V received a blow that damaged his crown during the battle.

evidence.quote: The king received an axe blow to the head, which knocked off a piece of the crown that formed part of his helmet.
Part of his crown was slashed off, but the young king managed to stay in the fight.

claims.claim: Heavily armored French knights drowned in the thick mud during the combat.

evidence.quote: some knights, encumbered by their armour, actually drowned in their helmets, including d'Albret.
Knights drowned in the mud or were stabbed by English archers

claims.claim: King Henry V ordered his men to execute French prisoners.

evidence.quote: Henry ordered the slaughter of most of the French prisoners,
English king then ordered his men to murder their prisoners for fear they would realize their advantage and counter-attack;

claims.claim: Around 6,000 French soldiers were killed during the battle.

evidence.quote: In all, around 6,000 of their fighting men were killed.
they left behind over 6,000 men dead in the mud of Agincourt.

claims.claim: English high-ranking casualties included the Duke of York and the Earl of Suffolk.

evidence.quote: These included the Duke of York, the young Earl of Suffolk
including the Duke of York and the Earl of Suffolk

claims.claim: French commander Charles d'Albret was killed during the battle.

evidence.quote: France lost its constable (Albret)
D’Albret was killed in the mud.

claims.claim: The Battle of Agincourt was immortalized in Shakespeare's play Henry V.

evidence.quote: The battle serves as the backdrop for notable works such as William Shakespeare's play Henry V
The Battle of Agincourt in 1415 was immortalized by Shakespeare in Henry V

claims.claim: The English longbowmen could strike targets from an extreme range of approximately 300 yards or meters.

evidence.quote: after the English longbowmen started shooting from extreme longbow range (approximately 300 yards (270 m)).
Their archers – equipped with longbows and capable of killing an enemy at nearly 300 metres –

claims.claim: The English forces at Agincourt were vastly outnumbered by the French army.

evidence.quote: The unexpected victory of the vastly outnumbered English troops over the French army
English outnumbered forces under Henry V defeated a French army.

claims.claim: The English army landed in northern France in August 1415.

evidence.quote: Henry's army landed in northern France on 13 August 1415,
sailed to Northern France and landed on August 13th.

disputed: The exact sizes of the English and French armies (ranging from traditional accounts of 25,000 French vs 5,700 English, to modern administrative revisions suggesting 12,000 French vs 9,000 English).
Whether the French boasted that they would cut off the fingers of captured English archers.
The exact number of English casualties, which contemporary accounts put as low as double digits, but other records state between 112 and 1,600.
The precise location of the battlefield (traditional site in the defile between Azincourt and Tramecourt versus theories suggesting a field west of Azincourt).
